newsitem.title: USA: R.I. policy curtails teen-age drinking parties.
newsitem.headline: R.I. policy curtails teen-age drinking parties.

text.p: At least a dozen parents in this Providence suburb have agreed to let police search their homes if they are out and authorities think their children are drinking alcohol, police said Friday.

To prevent teenage drinking, the police initiated a policy Wednesday requiring parents to sign a consent-to-search form giving them the right to knock on the door when parents are not at home if they suspect children are drinking alcohol. The police do not have to produce a warrant.
The local high school in this suburban community of 30,000 has a prom dance and graduation coming up, and "there will be an awful lot of partying," Cumberland police Sgt. Christine Crocker said.
"We've had at least a dozen parents return the release form so far and we're expecting a lot more," Cumberland police Sgt. Christine Crocker said.

The officers can make a visual search and if they spot alcoholic beverages "the party will be shut down and police will take down the name of every juvenile present and the parents will be notified," she said.
If the teenagers do not let in the police, "Well, they'll stay at the home. Sooner or later, those kids have to leave," she said.
Some see the policy, supported by the town's police chief and mayor, as an abrogation of the Constitution's Fourth Amendment, which guarantees citizens will be free from unreasonable searches.

"We're opposed to it," Steven Brown, executive director of the Rhode Island Civil Liberties Union, said. But he added it was unlikely the organisation would challenge the policy because it is voluntary.
"These parents are not forced to sign it. They are voluntarily waiving their rights."
Teenagers could not challenge the policy, he said. "As long as they're living in their parents' home, for the most part, their parents are signing their rights away."
What troubled Brown most, he said, was that "not only a neighbour, but someone with a grudge, a stranger, anyone" could alert the police and send them to a home.
